newsitem.title: CANADA: ATHLETICS-BAILEY APOLOGIZES FOR COMMENTS ABOUT JOHNSON.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-BAILEY APOLOGIZES FOR COMMENTS ABOUT JOHNSON.

text.p: Donovan Bailey and his camp were engaging in damage control on Monday, issuing an apology for the Canadian sprint star's comments about Michael Johnson following their 150-meter race on Sunday.

Bailey, the 100 meters Olympic champion and world record holder, won the hotly-anticipated head-to-head showdown in decidedly unsatisfying fashion when 200 meters Olympic gold medalist and world record holder Johnson pulled up injured and did not finish the race.

If the anti-climactic finish did not prove once and for all which man was the world's fasest, Bailey may have earned the title of world's most ungracious winner after all but accusing Johnson of faking the injury because he was losing the race and calling the American star a coward and a chicken.
"His comments were made in the heat of the battle," said Paul Donovan, one of Bailey's agents, on a day when numerous Canadian sportswriters were lambasting the sprinter's poor sportsmanship.
Bailey, the man who restored Canadian athletics honour eight years after the Ben Johnson steroid scandal, tarnished his own image both before and after Sunday's race.

He began the day by making excuses for a possible defeat even before the race by accusing organisers of "deceitfulness" and complaining about the layout of the special 150-meter track, saying he was running "under mental duress."
Then after a victory in the event that made him $1.5 million richer, he insulted Johnson on both Canadian and American television networks.
"He didn't pull up. He's a chicken. ... He's afaid to lose," Bailey told Canadian television.
"He didn't pull up. He's just a coward," Bailey reiterated for the U.S. TV counterpart.
Whether genuinely contrite or just feeling the need undo some of the damage to his image, Bailey reached out to Johnson through the media with an apology.
"I want to apologise to Michael Johnson for my post-race comments at the Toronto SkyDome," Bailey said in a statement.
"Michael and I began this unique event as friends, but the build-up to the race has left the friendship strained.
"I have tremendous respect for Michael's athletic ability and I hope that the injury he sustained is not-season threatening. I wish him a speedy return to competition."
Johnson, who refused to respond to Bailey's taunts after the race, said he had a pulled left thigh muscle.
Donovan said neither Bailey nor his agents had yet had a chance to apologise personally to Johnson.
